topicName: Kubernetes Networking Model and CNI Plugins
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Kubernetes Networking Model and CNI Plugins"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Kubernetes has a distinct and well-defined networking model that dictates how pods, nodes, and services communicate with one another. Unlike traditional virtual machine environments where networking is often configured manually, Kubernetes abstracts this layer through the Container Network Interface (CNI)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Principles of the Kubernetes Networking Model"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"All pods can communicate with all other pods on any node without using Network Address Translation (NAT)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"All agents on a node (like the kubelet) can communicate with all pods on that same node."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The IP that a pod sees as its own is the same IP that every other pod sees it as."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"What is CNI (Container Network Interface)?"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Container Network Interface is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project that consists of specifications and libraries for writing plugins to configure network interfaces in Linux containers. Kubernetes relies on CNI plugins to implement its networking model."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Popular CNI Plugins"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Calico: Known for performance, rich network policy support, and flexibility (supports both overlay and non-overlay networks)."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Flannel: A very simple, overlay-based CNI plugin that is easy to set up, making it ideal for development clusters."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cilium: Uses eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) to provide high-performance networking, security, and visibility."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Installing a CNI Plugin Example"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Typically, a CNI plugin is installed via a Kubernetes Manifest file applied to the cluster using kubectl. Below is an example of applying a network provider manifest."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/coreos/flannel/master/Documentation/kube-flannel.yml"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Verifying CNI Installation"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once the CNI plugin is deployed, you can verify that the network pods are running correctly in the kube-system namespace by executing the following command:"},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=flannel"}]
